# Prompting Qwen Image

Models: Qwen Image 3.0. A good prompt runs about 1500 characters.

Name each reference where the prompt uses it as `@{ref:<ref>}`, with the exact ref you pass; Sceneform swaps in the model's own token, so wherever this guide names a token (`@Image1`, `Figure 1`), write the mention instead.

Qwen Image 3.0 takes long, literal prompts and is strongest at text and dense layouts. Sceneform sends the prompt with Qwen's own rewriting switched off, so the model sees exactly what you write: every decision you leave out is the model's to make.

**Order.** Lead with the subject, then composition and framing, then the environment, then the light, then the style. Opening with style makes the subject serve the adjectives. Write full descriptive sentences; a few short style terms can close the prompt.

**Be specific.** A short prompt hands every choice to the model: "a bakery counter" comes back as a generic display case. Counts and positions are honoured when you state them; vague quantities such as "some pastries" give the model licence it will use.

**Framing follows the canvas.** The aspect ratio changes what gets composed, not only how it is cropped: a square frames the shopfront, a wide frame lets the street in, a tall frame shows the upper storey. Write a composition the chosen shape can hold.

**Text in the image.** Qwen renders Chinese, English and ten more languages, legible down to small type. Quote every string that must appear and say where it sits: anything you do not quote, the model writes for you. Give hierarchy by relation, never by measurement: "large bold capitals across the upper third", "a smaller line directly beneath", not point sizes or pixel positions. Write non-Latin copy in its own characters; asking for a headline that "means" something produces script that only looks right. For mixed scripts, say "on the same line" for every row that pairs them. When the copy is the point, close with "no other text". When the user wants no lettering at all, say "no text", because Qwen adds lettering readily.

**Dense layouts.** Infographics, menus, front pages, spec sheets and interface mocks are where the long prompt pays off. Brief it like a designer: name the sheet, then the title block, then each region in reading order with its copy quoted. The order you write is the order it lays out. Tie each grid cell to its position ("top left cell, headed ..."), list table rows in order, and state the shared style once at the start.

**Edits and several images.** Up to three images. Name each by its token and what it holds in the same phrase: "the leather satchel from image 2", "the empty room from image 3". Give every image a job: three images with no roles come back as an average of all three. For an edit, name what changes and what holds: "make the bottle amber; keep the exact cylindrical shape, the exact proportions, the plain warm grey backdrop". When a product moves into a new scene, restate its material, colour and hardware rather than trusting the image alone. Objects come back intact; busy rooms are re-rendered and drift.

**Exclusions.** Keep what the user excluded in plain words inside the prompt: "no people, no readable text".

**Avoid.** Describing copy instead of quoting it. Absolute sizes or coordinates. Paraphrasing or translating text that must render. Exclusions for things the scene never had.
